pr_title: Add Fetch All Replies Part 1: Backend
pr_body:
Fix: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/9409
Fix: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/14017
Fix: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/18150


Original PR Here: https://github.com/NeuromatchAcademy/mastodon/pull/44
Further description here: https://github.com/NeuromatchAcademy/mastodon/issues/43

I've never made a PR for upstream before, so forgive me if i'm doing it wrong <3

## Problem

Currently, instances only receive posts a) if someone on the instance follows the post author or follows someone who boosts a post, b) if someone explicitly searches for a post url, or c) the instance fetches it though a relay. This means that for most posts, someone on an instance that different from the OP of a thread only has a partial view of the replies.

This creates the following problems:

- We are missing an important discovery mechanism: if you or someone you know doesn't already know someone, then you might never find them, even if you're frequently responding to the same things. 
- One of the direct causes of the well known "a thousand of the same reply" problem, where since people can't see what's already been said will say the same thing. This is *exhausting* for even moderately sized accounts, and I think in no small part contributes to the perception of the fediverse as a bunch of persnickety reply guys
- Disadvantages smaller instances: the fediverse can feel very quiet on smaller instances, and I (and other small instance dwellers) will almost always open the original instance post to see the replies since i see a tiny fraction of them. This runs into the further problem that if i am logged out on that instance I can only see 60 replies anyway, so there really is no way for someone on a smaller instance to see a full reply tree aka a full discussion.
- It makes us unable to realize the actual power of distributed moderation, where because only a person on the same server as someone receiving abuse can see it, we can't allow other people on other servers to report things, defray the labor of moderation, and potentially avoid the receivers of abuse from seeing it altogether: https://neuromatch.social/@jonny/113486017955301019 This has been noted uncountably many times as one of the manifestations of the racism of the fediverse, see e.g.: https://hachyderm.io/@mekkaokereke/112536749737121291

## Approach

- When a post is expanded, a call is made to the `context` endpoint
- After the `context` endpoint renders, if we `Status.should_fetch_replies` and the `context` request is made by a logged in user, we trigger a `FetchAllRepliesWorker`
- The `FetchAllRepliesWorker` will recursively expand the reply tree, gathering the URIs of the statuses to fetch using a `FetchAllRepliesService`
- The `FetchAllRepliesService` will
  - Reject URIs for statuses that a) already exist in the db, and b) have had their replies fetched recently
  - Update the last fetched time for any statuses that *do* exist in the DB so they won't be double-fetched
- The `FetchAllRepliesService` then bulk-pushes thsoe URIs to `FetchReplyWorker` and from there on we are back in existing implementation territory.

## Likely Concerns

### Privacy

- **Viewer privacy:** The fetch all replies worker/service uses the `Account.representative` user to sign all requests, rather than the account that is making the `context` request so that it doesn't behave like an unexpected "read receipt." 
- **Poster privacy:** Responding instances will only serve replies that are publicly broadcastable (i.e. no followers-only or direct posts). All other visibility controls are unaffected and apply to all fetched replies. Previously I had considered making a special delegated user for fetching replies so that concerned instances could block the fetch all replies behavior specifically, rather than blocking the instance delegate. We may want to explore other ways that instances can refuse fetch all reply requests if they want to.
 
As an addendum, I would say that this should be considered *expected behavior* for activitypub: the `replies` collection is a public `Collection` that is part of an actor's `outbox` and servers should expect other servers to to paginate through these, and the source servers should implement access controls accordingly.

### DoS/Amplification

I tried to handle this by adding cooldowns and limits to all the relevant parameters, but lmk if they are not enough.

More notes:

- The behavior is only triggered when someone explicitly signals that they want to view a post and its replies, i.e. when the `context` endpoint is called, so this is not called for all posts.
- The behavior *does* launch a large number of sidekiq jobs, but these are empirically completed quite quickly, at least if an instance has their sidekiq configuration set up to use multiple processes (which should be the default)
- The behavior is recursively deduplicated - each status has its own 'last fetched' time, so re-triggering a fetch of the parent status or different parts of the tree doesn't cause duplicated recursive fetches. The update of the 'last fetched' time happens when the status is *queued* for fetching, rather than when the fetch happens, so the window for duplicating a fetch is very small and probably in practice nonexistent.

Hi! Thanks for your PR!

I haven't actually reviewed it yet, but going on through the description, you've already given this a lot of thought and seem to have taken a sensible approach. I'd like to highlight a few concerns though:
- crawling reply collections is likely to increase the number of occurrences of posts being fetched without the source server keeping track of who has fetched it, increasing the risk for an `Update` or `Delete` activity about that post not reaching every server that knows about the post
- recursively fetching replies can easily add up in terms of work and create a lot of load both for the local server and for the remote requested ones, especially since ingesting a post may lead to fetching its author, then fetching its featured collection, fetching mentioned accounts and so on. I'm worried about this, but at least a quick glance at the implementation does not reveal any unbounded recursion here, and I guess at some point we'll have to try and see how well this performs

I thought I had elaborated on that, but apparently I haven't. Currently, fetching a post that has been deleted will just return a 404 and not do anything. There are a few considerations about that (related, <https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/10640#issuecomment-2442039804>):
- private posts that you do not have access to (not very relevant for our current discussion of public replies, but the mechanisms still need to be considered, since otherwise an attacker could e.g. list private posts in their replies list as an attempt to get them deleted) return 404 as well to not confirm the existence of the post
- we *could* return 410 and optionally a tombstone object for actually-deleted posts, but that would disclose that a post made at that time (the time is encoded in the post ID) previously existed, which could be considered a sensitive piece of information. I would argue that this wouldn't be an issue for the majority of users, but I'm unsure about changing that since it's a concern that is difficult to convey to people for whom this may matter

We worry about two things:

First, the amount of server-to-server requests that this could cause and the impact on the infrastructure. This can be solved by refreshing the statuses periodically (and updating the client if they changed) for edits, but it poses an issue with deletion.

At the moment, if you query a status that has been deleted, you have no way to know if the status existed but has been deleted, if you are not allowed to see it, or if it never existed. Ok so the issue is that since nobody on an instance who has fetched a status via fetch all replies follows the poster, they wont get updates and deletes.

The update part of that seems straightforward - when a post is expanded when viewed again, fetching it should be already be treated as an update event. That should already be handled by this PR (actually I need to update it to fetch the root post too after the PR where we started using boost/fave totals from AP collections, because it would be confusing if all the counts were correct *except* the root post). In general I favor the "on demand" update pattern more than polling, though I acknowledge it requires us to double tap in some cases.

And i see the problem with deletion. It also seems related to the future implementation of reply controls - where we will need to consult the host instance about what replies it acknowledges so we can exclude replies even if we know about them through other means if the host instance doesnt want them displayed.

I think an "affirmative no" on the existence of a status via a tombstone makes sense, because the only means by which we will have fetched that reply via this mechanism is a case where the instance representative actor is authorized to fetch it, so it should also be authorized to see the tombstone, no? Seems like this should already be an issue for posts that are fetched via search, because that's fetched with a request thats marked as on behalf of the searching user (or the "find the first account that follows the posting account" approach ive seen elsewhere)? It seems like 404s during fetch all could be disambiguated using that pattern too: if we're fetching a reply and get a 404, try again by requesting it on behalf of the first user on instance who follows them. In both cases, if no such user exists (we shouldnt have the post), or one does (we should be authorized to see it if it exists) and we still get a 404, then delete. A 3rd server shouldnt be able to force us to delete (except in the future with reply controls, but thats separate question) since we always are asking the instance hosting that reply.

Lmk what of that you'd like me to tackle here or in an accessory PR, im eager to move forward on this because of the frequency with which I am being tagged in threads where someone has been saying not having this is super bad for them. 

> First, the amount of server-to-server requests that this could cause and the impact on the infrastructure. 

The configurable timeouts and limits and etc. Are supposed to allow a fetching instance to control how much resources fetch all replies uses, and I assume the already existing ratelimiting system should handle the other side. But there are tons of ways that this could be made more efficient with more tweaks to the way masto does AP that I would be happy to tackle in follow on PRs.

- one is that masto currently inlines all the replies, which is super expensive and wasteful since we still always need to fetch it from the origin server. Simplifying the replies collection to just be a collection of URIs would be a big first step to making things cheaper. 
- we also could batch fetch requests - rather than requesting each status individually, we could collect all the URIs we want from another instance and request them all at once. For that we could create an additional Linked Data term and put it in the instance serializer, and instances that supported batched AP collection requests could advtertise that in their instance properties
- I *think* that the replies collection is already straight up reverse chron, except for putting self-replies first? We could also use the last fetched at timestamp in the request for the replies collection, and the other instance could then only send us statuses that have been updated, created, or deleted since that time. Same thing re: instance advertising capabilities.
- similarly, when we fetch a status, we could include a header that signals when the last time we fetched it was, and if there have been no new replies or changes to the status then the other instance could just signal "you're up to date" without serving the whole status.

Point being that I think fetch all replies is a must-fix behavior, and that we can mitigate perf problems either through limits or improving efficiency once we see how those bottlenecks show themselves. I would be happy to write a page in the docs on fetch all replies config to make it obvious how to diagnose problems and adjust the settings if instanced are being overwhelmed.

That seems sensible, but just to make sure: how do you decide to re-fetch a possibly deleted post? If it's deleted, it would typically not be in the replies collection, so is the idea to retry all public replies that you know of but were not returned by the replies collection crawl, in addition to those returned?

Also, Mastodon returns a 403 for temporarily-suspended users, so that is not a concern, but I suspect other software might return a 404. If that's the case, temporary moderation decisions could have much bigger effects by making replies (and associated information, like bookmarks, or favorites and boosts that you couldn't undo) disappear.

Another related concern that came up recently is moderation-related: if an abusive reply gets fetched this way, a lot more servers may be exposed to it, but the number of servers made aware of any suspension at origin (before the complete deletion of the account) would not increase. This issue is different from post edition and deletion because the distribution paths are different (and more of an issue currently, see #33053). I suppose this can be addressed by also re-fetching every author account when fetching posts, but this could quickly add up.

And a final concern is the behavior when reaching `request_id`-based limits: associated data (mentions, parent posts, moved-to-account, …) is simply not fetched, and the information that it was here to begin with is completely lost. Right! I was pitching one way we could do that. Another would be to just take the diff of the reply collection as reported by the server and the one we have locally. that would be pretty fast, and would also be pretty generic - when we get a replies collection (ie. the collection doesn't 401 or 404) we should treat that as the canonical representation of the replies that should exist, which also gets us reply controls for free (edit: as in any other software could implement arbitrary reply controls by just excluding posts from reply collections, which is spec compliant even if the response to it is unspecified by activitypub/streams, not the other parts like ux/moderation/etc.).

> “the first account that follows the posting account” (mainly because there is no generic way to do that… although we could have heuristics).

I was referring to this: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/blob/360b6d3a442c1a95e073043e0d62e46ead7728a2/app/services/activitypub/fetch_featured_collection_service.rb#L103

not as a preferred option, but as one that has precedent and is another pitch for a heuristic, yes.

> But fetching a post via search is kind of an edge case, the PR here would generalize the behavior and the issue.

I think it resolves the issue! if we then visit that post after searching (or any other means), fetch all replies allows us to synchronize state with the external server(s) rather than the current behavior of doing nothing.

> That seems sensible, but just to make sure: how do you decide to re-fetch a possibly deleted post? If it's deleted, it would typically not be in the replies collection, so is the idea to retry all public replies that you know of but were not returned by the replies collection crawl, in addition to those returned?

All posts are re-fetched. 

- If a post is not in the replies collection, that means that the instance or the account being replied to doesn't want it in the replies collection (or they won't give us a replies collection, at which point we do nothing on refetch, but also would not have received any posts that we wouldn't receive deletion activities for via fetch all replies so there is nothing to do), so we would remove the "in reply to" value for that post.
- If we attempt to re-fetch a post and the origin server doesn't acknowledge it, then that means it has been deleted by the origin server or the OP and the secondary effects of the posts like bookmarks etc. should be removed. This would also be pretty simple to filter to be conservative - we only delete a post on a 404 if nobody on our instance follows them. if we do, then we shouldn't delete because we should have received the delete. Otherwise, we either got the post from fetch all replies or from search, and the fetch all replies behavior is strictly additive.

> Another related concern that came up recently is moderation-related: if an abusive reply gets fetched this way, a lot more servers may be exposed to it, but the number of servers made aware of any suspension at origin (before the complete deletion of the account) would not increase. This issue is different from post edition and deletion because the distribution paths are different (and more of an issue currently, see https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/33053). I suppose this can be addressed by also re-fetching every author account when fetching posts, but this could quickly add up.

- More servers seeing abusive replies could be [useful for moderation](https://hachyderm.io/@mekkaokereke/112536749737121291), particularly with the work on forwarding reports, because otherwise only the recipient of the abuse sees it and has to deal with it
- Same as above, if origin server 404's a post, we could have a secondary path that could check on the account being suspended, and then discover the suspension that way, which also prevents any other abusive replies from that account being seen on the fetching instance, which would otherwise wait for other mechanisms to refresh the account. Doing it on demand is not additional work, but moves up work that would be done in another way later, and since it's a terminal event doesn't incur future work.

So these are
- Public/unlisted statuses
- From accounts followed by nobody on the fetching instance
- Optionally: In reply to a status that is currently being viewed. (edit: this is implicit when we are handling a replies collection, but the scope would just be for the above two)

Let's call these "fetch-only" statuses, and this should be a scope within the `FetchRepliesConcern`

Which means that, in this PR, we don't need to worry about
- followers-only/DM statuses - we won't get them by fetching public collections
- statuses from accounts with at least one follower on the fetching instance - we should receive deletions/updates as normal. edit: since we don't have reply controls yet, replies from instance A to a status on instance B as viewed by instance C will be displayed even if instance B removes them by moderation already if anyone in instance C follows the account on instance A, so we should handle that in a separate PR.

## Pitch for handling remotely removed statuses

So for handling updates/deletions, that leaves these cases (i think?):

| local state | remote state                                                 | behavior                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| unfetched   | normal                                                       | fetch!                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| normal      | normal                                                       | do nothing                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| outdated    | normal                                                       | update, with cooldown                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| normal      | removed by origin (permanent)                                | (1) |
| normal      | removed by origin (temporary)                                |  (2)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| normal      |  removed by replied-to instance (permanent), normal at origin | (3)                                                                                                                                                                                 |

(1)
- diff replies against fetched collection
- filter to "extra" statuses that are...
  - public/unlisted replies that we have
  - missing from collection
  - have no followers on fetching instance
- attempt to fetch "extra" statuses
- receive 404
- remove status, preserving it
- trigger account refresh (in case the whole account was suspended)
- in 30d, attempt to fetch again, if still 404, remove completely

(2)
- ... (as above)
- receive 403 or 404 (depending on software)
- ...

(3)
- ...
- receive 200
- ...

So recalling that we only need to handle statuses that are reachable only by fetch all replies - i.e. public/unlisted && statuses from accounts that have zero followers on the fetching instance - I think all three cases of statuses removed remotely, either from moderation or voluntarily, should all behave similarly: remove the status without destroying (i.e. with the `preserve` option here: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/blob/be43b01eb11cc5bc134942f8d9725d20734349cf/app/services/remove_status_service.rb#L156 ), and then in whatever period of time we want to hang onto it in case the removal was temporary (i put 30d as a placeholder), check to see if its back, and then trash it then otherwise. I haven't looked if there is already a scheduled service for this, but can write one if there isn't.

## responding to comments

> This is for fetching someone's featured collection service

I was only mentioning this to say that there is some precedent for making a request on behalf of an account rather than the instance representative, but since we shouldn't be handling private/followers only posts i think that may have been distracting for me to bring it up, so we can forget about this for now i think :)

> Wrt. the replies collection being the complete and unique source of truth for what is in a collection, I'm afraid this would work very poorly with private replies and DMs. Granted, only public posts matter for fetching, but it either means you can't just remove non-public posts that are marked as a reply,

yes! as above, we should only consider public/unlisted posts from accounts that have no local followers for removal, since those are the only ones that would come from fetch all replies in the first place.

> There is also the issue of the collection possibly being too big to process

hmm ya, so this would be the case where, for a single post, we reach the local or global rate limit for fetching replies, then all of the oldest (i.e. in the bottom of reverse chron collection) posts would be ambiguous re: whether they should be removed or not. 

I think there are (at least) three separable cases there:
- (1) adversarial replied-to status: an attacker spoofs an expensive replies collection
- (2) adversarial replies: an attacker spams a ton of replies to a well-behaved status
- (3) normal limits: the fetching instance has set a very low local/global fetch limit

and the thing that we want to avoid is displaying replies that have been removed due to moderation. 

I think we can treat (1)/(2) as handled by other means of moderation: we should ban/block adversarial instances or spam accounts, which would then mean that the worst case is someone scrolling down through all the spam and seeing an extra reply during the cooldown between fetching.  

For (3), the only problem case is for a reply from instance A to a status on instance B when viewed by instance C that has been removed by moderation by instance B *after* we fetched it previously. The other cases - removed by instance A - we should be able to handle as above. 

Since we would only know about such statuses by having been told by instance B about them previously, there isn't an additional privacy concern about being able to ask about them again specifically. It seems like maybe we want to have some query parameter for the replies collection that allows us to ask whether some specific URIs are in that collection, so something like

```js
query_uris = [
  "example.com/1",
  "example.com/2",
]

response = {
  "example.com/1": false,
  "example.com/2": true,
}
```

That would probably be a whole lot more efficient than going out and trying to refetch them all from third party servers too, and resolves some questions about implicitness in incomplete collections. That would only work for masto<->masto since it's not in the AP spec, but it would be better than nothing? It seems worth a FEP to have a "query if collection contains x" because it seems p important for usable collections, since they should be the source of truth but face practical limitations of not having infinite time to page/adversarial actors.

Alternatively, we could return some indicator that we stopped fetching a collection because we hit a rate limit (the size of the returned collection being == to the passed limit would work, if implicit), and either continue paging if we have "extra" fetch-only replies, hide those extras, etc.

## summary

- make scope for "fetch-only" statuses: only the statuses that would have come from fetching replies/search/etc.: public/unlisted statuses from accounts that have no followers on the fetching instance.
- handle "extra" fetch-only statuses that are known by the fetching instance but not in the remote replies collection by temporarily removing them.
  - probably outside the scope of this PR: additionally trigger a refresh of the account in case it has been suspended.
- probably outside the scope of this PR: potentially add a query method to check if statuses are in a collection

issue_context.title: UI button to "see all conversation" using context API
issue_context.body:
### Pitch

I think this has been talked about before in threads like https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/14017 and https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/3794

Essentially when viewing a toot on a small instance you are often missing replies because your instance never saw them - this is totally reasonable and expected behaviour, once you get how AP works. 

However if you view the web version of the original-toot and search for the URLs of a few reply-toots then your server knows about them and you can then see them in your view of the conversation around the original-toot.  Again very reasonable and expected behaviour.

What I am suggesting is an UI button of some kind that trips an API call (so it can be done from 3rd party clients) for my instance to contact the originating toots instance and ask for the URLs of all replies to the original-toot.  Then essentially my instance does a search on them, adding them to its pool of known toots and finally refreshes the page I'm viewing - hence they appear and I have an up to date view of the conversation from inside my own instance and can easily boost/favourite/reply to them.

Retrieving toots from remote servers clearly works, and there is already [GET /api/v1/statuses/:id/context](https://docs.joinmastodon.org/methods/statuses/#parent-and-child-statuses) which presumably could be used to pull in the conversation so I think the only thing missing is a piece of UI glue to trigger this all to happen and/or adding an API call that binds all this behaviour together (which would make it easier for 3rd party clients) and then add a UI button that sits on top of that single "fetch context" or "see all conversation" API call.

Additionally I think at least a subset of people would find it useful/accessible to have a per-profile option to automatically make this API call (if its not been called in the past X minutes for this toot) when viewing a single toot, as that way they can know they are getting an up date view of conversation on the fedi around that toot.

### Motivation

- Removes behaviour that is confusing for new or less technical users.
- Makes for a more actual and global view of conversation flow be available on small instances.  
- Removes the need for constantly going to the web view of a remote instance, scanning the replies, then working out where to hit reply from there, getting redirected back to your original instance in a popup to type the reply, etc.etc.etc.

It appears some clients have started using this technique, calling the public /statuses/:id/context endpoint on the remote server.  The problem with this is that if the client renders the toots directly from the context response then it effectively bypasses blocks.  I don't know if any clients are doing that, but it is a concern.

Maybe it would be helpful to have an API call similar to /statuses/:id/context that fetched only enough information to allow the toots to be searched for via the user's local server?  This could then be used explicitly for this purpose, reducing the size of the response from the foreign server, and also reducing the likelihood of admins blocking API access due to concerns about clients bypassing blocks.

> The problem with this is that […] it effectively bypasses blocks.

To add context to this, there appears to be a sizeable contingent of people who have come to understand blocking to mean denying read access *globally* rather than merely refusing interaction with their instance, who are [suddenly appalled](https://cloudisland.nz/@aurynn/109773984132195304) to learn that their public posts are readable by the unauthenticated public. If you hold this perspective, it follows that general-purpose clients and web browsers are actually block circumvention tools that need to be cracked down on.

> there appears to be a sizeable contingent of people who have come to understand blocking to mean denying read access _globally_ rather than merely refusing interaction with their instance

This is one concern, and was part of what led me to suggest a way for a client to read less data from a foreign instance.  But I think the bigger concern here is for user safety.

If a client is fetching toots directly from a foreign instance, then the normal filtering that is applied by the local server is not done.  It's now on the client not to show the user harmful content that the local instance would normally have filtered out for them - either replies from users on an instance that is blocked by the local instance but not the foreign instance, or from users that the fetching user has explicitly blocked.

Therefore, the client should always check to see whether toots that it has pulled from a foreign server are accessible from the local server - but given the public API that allows the client to find the context toots also fetches all the content it would be tempting as a client not to do this.

Clearly a better fix would be to make Mastodon server propagate replies so this functionality was unnecessary, but that is a much more complex fix so client workarounds like this seem inevitable in the short term.

I think having a low recursion limit makes sense. Every request is costly (up to a few seconds of waiting on a remote server), and the more we do in the service, the longer we will keep a worker busy. This can easily become a DoS vector.

As for paginating the context, yes, that would be extremely useful, and it could be useful in this specific case as well, but as you may have noticed this is a massively complex issue that also involves a lot of UX considerations (for instance, Mastodon's display of replies is “flattened” so the pagination cutoffs are far less obvious to represent than on say, reddit)

Checking on how we are meaning recursion here, just because activitystreams also refers to just iterating through collection pages as recursion: do we mean a limit on paging or do we mean limiting the recursion depth within a reply tree (only get e.g. `depth<n` replies)?

To me a limit on paging makes perfect sense as a complementary limit to the max statuses limit, but a depth in reply tree recursion is in my opinion undesirable: In practice i have been seeing a pretty even distribution between deep and broad trees, and since there is no paging in the context endpoint, the experience for both being "i go to the status, and a few seconds later I refresh, and all the replies are there" is ... great! Since the action is implicit on loading the context endpoint, and we don't have the ux pieces in place for "see more replies" and recursively expanding trees, I would think that some invisible barrier where someone finds out later 'oh i wasn't actually seeing all the replies, i needed to click around more' would be pretty frustrating.

I think the max page limit handles concerns re: runtime/resource usage in either case of deep and broad trees well, and does it more directly - we care about the number of requests/pages, not the depth of trees per se, the depth of trees is just a proxy for that.

For the sake of having it in thread (assuming you have read it, but for the benefit of passers-by the haven't), the way the service works is that there is one long-running `FetchAllRepliesWorker`. That is just getting a list of URIs to fetch from the replies collections. It then hands off those URIs in batches to sets of `FetchReplyWorker`s. So the long-running worker should be mostly I/O bound as you say. We have found it necessary to [modify the sidekiq queues](https://wiki.neuromatch.social/Performance#Sidekiq) when we were as small as a few dozen users, so that might be a thing worth exploring making default separately if we are concerned about long running workers clogging up slots. Otherwise, it makes sense to me for this worker to be one of the main things that occupies the `pull` queue, as most of the rest of the things that use it are even more background-oriented tasks than this is - the one that we see running most commonly are the `SynchronizeFeatured*Collection` workers.

I think this makes sense to make configurable rather than setting a hard limit - for small instances, they probably want to have a higher limit because they are the ones most impacted by not seeing replies, don't have a million users requesting threads, and can let a worker linger for longer. for large instances, they probably want to set the page limit lower, etc.
